evidence.claim: An FDA-issued certificate is required for lawful operation of a mammography facility subject to MQSA; to obtain it, a facility must meet the § 900.12 quality standards and be accredited by an approved accreditation body or other FDA-designated entity.
evidence.scope: Facilities under U.S. regulatory jurisdiction providing mammography.
evidence.exceptions: Department of Veterans Affairs facilities are excluded (§ 900.10). States approved as certification agencies may certify facilities (Subpart C).
evidence.excerpt: After October 1, 1994, a certificate issued by FDA is required for lawful operation of all mammography facilities subject to the provisions of this subpart. To obtain a certificate from FDA, facilities are required to meet the quality standards in § 900.12 and to be accredited by an approved accreditation body or other entity as designated by FDA.

evidence.locator: NCI Mammograms fact sheet, What is a mammogram? (updated 2025-12-02)
evidence.claim: Screening mammograms look for breast cancer before symptoms. Diagnostic mammograms evaluate a lump or other change found by the patient or clinician. The same machines are used; diagnostic exams usually include images from more angles and therefore a higher radiation dose.
evidence.excerpt: Mammograms are used for breast cancer screening because they can find tumors at an earlier stage, before they cause symptoms. Mammograms can also be used to check for breast cancer after a woman or her doctor finds a lump or other change. This type of mammogram is called a diagnostic mammogram. The same machines are used for both types of mammograms. However, diagnostic mammography requires images from more angles than screening mammography, so the dose of radiation is higher.

evidence.locator: USPSTF Breast Cancer Screening final recommendation (April 30, 2024), Clinician Summary — To whom does this recommendation apply?
evidence.claim: The 2024 USPSTF recommendation applies to cisgender women and other persons assigned female at birth age 40+ at average risk, and also to those with factors such as a first-degree family history or dense breasts. It does not apply to persons with high-risk genetic markers/syndromes, high-dose chest radiation at a young age, previous breast cancer, or a high-risk breast lesion on prior biopsy.
evidence.scope: Who the USPSTF average-risk recommendation covers.
evidence.excerpt: These recommendations apply to cisgender women and all other persons assigned female at birth (including transgender men and nonbinary persons) 40 years or older at average risk of breast cancer. They also apply to women who have factors associated with an increased risk of breast cancer, such as a family history of breast cancer (ie, a first-degree relative with breast cancer) or having dense breasts. These recommendations do not apply to persons who have a genetic marker or syndrome associated with a high risk of breast cancer (eg, BRCA1 or BRCA2 genetic variation), a history of high-dose radiation therapy to the chest at a young age, or previous breast cancer or a high-risk breast lesion on previous biopsies.
